before.title: CD4E 4-speed automatic transmission premature failure
before.description: The Ford-designed CD4E automatic transaxle fitted to 1993-1997 (5th-gen GE) 626s with an automatic is one of the most notorious weak points of the car. It runs hot, has undersized clutch packs and a fragile forward-clutch/valve-body design, and commonly fails anywhere from 60,000-100,000 miles. Both the FS 2.0L I4 and KL 2.5L V6 automatic cars used it. Repair shops have reported very high failure rates and the NHTSA/CarComplaints logs are dominated by transmission complaints for these years. A primary root cause was an inadequate factory transmission cooling circuit (a poorly designed radiator that did a bad job cooling the ATF). There was no recall, so owners bore the cost. The 626/MX-6 community regards a manual-transmission car as far more reliable.
before.solution: Preventatively, service the fluid every 30k miles with the correct spec fluid and add an auxiliary transmission cooler; heat is the primary killer. Once slipping, flashing O/D light, or harsh/erratic shifting begins, a proper rebuild with an upgraded/updated valve body and clutch parts (or a quality remanufactured unit) is the accepted repair. A band-aid fluid change rarely saves a unit that is already slipping.

proposal.title: CD4E 4-speed automatic transmission premature failure

Those records support the symptom pattern, but they do not prove a universal CD4E failure rate, a fixed mileage window, the same transmission behind every listed engine, or the previously stated clutch, valve-body and radiator design causes. proposal.solution: If the overdrive light flashes, the transmission slips, shifts harshly or loses drive, limit driving and have a qualified transmission technician record codes, fluid condition and level, line pressure, commanded gear and cooler flow before choosing a repair. Verify the installed transmission by VIN and tag. For a 1997 vehicle receiving an overhaul or replacement unit, Mazda TSB 05-002/21 requires a technician to inspect and power-flush the cooler and lines so debris from the prior failure does not damage the replacement. Do not buy an auxiliary cooler, solenoid, valve body or rebuilt transmission from this page; the installed unit and failure mode must be confirmed first.

before.title: Distributor Internal Coil and Hall Effect Sensor Failure
before.description: The 626's distributor assembly contains the ignition coil and hall effect sensor, both of which fail prematurely. The distributor is mounted on the rear of the cylinder head where it is exposed to engine heat. Internal components fail between 80,000-120,000 miles causing intermittent no-start, misfires, and stalling. The failure is often intermittent, making diagnosis difficult.
before.solution: Replace the complete distributor assembly ($200-$400). Replacing only the cap and rotor will not fix internal electronic failures. A remanufactured distributor from Cardone is a reliable budget option. Verify the coil wire resistance and check for spark at each cylinder before condemning the distributor. The ignition control module (ICM) should also be tested, as it can cause similar symptoms.

Hard starting when engine is hot

before.title: Head gasket failure / chronic overheating (age and cooling neglect)
before.description: Both the FS 2.0L I4 and KL 2.5L V6 are prone to head gasket failure as they age, almost always downstream of a cooling-system problem: original radiators clog, plastic end-tanks crack, thermostats stick, and water pumps weep, letting the engine overheat and compromising the gasket (or cracking/warping a head). Symptoms range from coolant loss and white exhaust smoke to oil/coolant intermixing and heavy oil burning on badly failed engines. Because these are inexpensive older cars, deferred cooling maintenance is the usual root cause rather than a specific factory defect.
before.solution: Address cooling health proactively: replace an old radiator, thermostat, water pump and hoses, and never let the car run hot. Once a gasket is blown, the accepted repair is a full head gasket job with the head checked for flatness/cracks and resurfaced as needed; on the V6 both heads and the timing belt/seals should be done together while the front of the engine is open.
symptoms: Recurring coolant loss with no visible leak
Heavy oil burning and loud intake noise

before.title: Ignition switch overheating / fire hazard (NHTSA recall 15V674000)
before.description: The ignition switch on 1993-1998 626s (and many other Mazdas of the era) was assembled with an excessive amount of grease at the internal contact points. Over time and with heat, the grease can carbonize, become conductive, and cause the contacts to overheat, reducing insulation and producing smoke and, in the worst case, a fire. Mazda issued NHTSA recall 15V674000 covering roughly 1.37 million vehicles, including the 626; the recall began December 17, 2015. Many original owners never received notice by the time these cars reached second/third hands, so a large share are still unremedied.
before.solution: This is a free manufacturer recall repair: an authorized Mazda dealer replaces the ignition switch at no cost. Owners can verify open recall status by VIN on the NHTSA or Mazda owner site. If a dealer can no longer source the part, be alert to switch-area heat/odor; independent replacement of the switch contact block is the aftermarket fix.
symptoms: Smoke or burning smell from the ignition switch/steering column
Ignition switch hot to the touch

proposal.title: Ignition switch overheating / fire hazard (NHTSA recall 15V674000)

before.title: KL V6 distributor internal oil seal leak / cap-and-rotor fouling
before.description: The 2.5L KL-DE V6 uses a cam-driven distributor with an internal O-ring/oil seal at the base and a shaft bushing. As the seal hardens with age, engine oil weeps up the shaft and pools inside the distributor cap, fouling the cap and rotor and shorting the ignition. On higher-mileage cars the shaft bushing also wears, allowing shaft wobble that both worsens the leak and disturbs the pickup signal. The result is a rough-running, misfiring, hard-starting or stalling V6 that many owners chase before finding the source. This is a well-known KL-engine quirk shared with the MX-6 and Ford Probe GT.
before.solution: First-line fix is replacing the cheap base O-ring/seal (a few dollars) plus a fresh cap and rotor and cleaning the shaft, which cures most cases; applying a little sealer at the cap on reinstall helps. If the distributor shaft has visible play/wobble, the whole distributor must be replaced (reman ~$150-300 plus labor). Keeping oil out of the cap also prolongs plug-wire and coil life.
symptoms: Oil pooled inside the distributor cap

before.title: Rough idle / stalling from idle air control valve and intake manifold gasket
before.description: A very common driveability complaint on the 626 is an unstable idle that surges, dips, or stalls at stops, most often caused by a sticking or dirty idle air control (IAC) valve and, on higher-mileage cars, leaking intake manifold gaskets that create unmetered vacuum leaks (the gasket often leaks on the underside where it is not visible from above). The problem is worsened by carbon buildup in the throttle body. It affects both the FS I4 and KL V6, and because these are age/mileage-driven wear items rather than a single defect, it shows up across the whole 1990s run.
before.solution: Clean or replace the IAC valve, clean the throttle body, and inspect/replace the intake manifold gasket if a vacuum leak is confirmed (smoke or carb-cleaner test). Check all vacuum lines first. These fixes are inexpensive parts with modest labor and typically restore a stable idle.
symptoms: Stalling at stops or when coming to a stop

before.title: Timing belt auto-tensioner spring failure (1998 NHTSA recall)
before.description: On 1998 626s an external spring in the timing-belt automatic tensioner can break, and the broken spring fragment can get caught in the timing belt. This can cause the belt to jump/skip and the engine to stall unexpectedly. Mazda recalled affected vehicles; owner notification began September 28, 2000. Separate from the recall, the 626's timing belt is a routine wear item (roughly 60,000-mile replacement) and neglecting it risks serious engine damage on the interference V6, so this era of car frequently needs belt/tensioner/water-pump service simply due to age.
before.solution: For the recall, an authorized dealer inspects the tensioner and replaces it free if it is an affected unit. As general maintenance, replace the timing belt, tensioner and idler, the cam/crank seals and the water pump together at the service interval; the FS is a non-interference design but the V6 job is more involved and should be done by the book.
symptoms: Broken tensioner spring found during service

before.title: CD4E Automatic Transmission Failure
before.description: The 1998-2002 626 uses the Ford CD4E automatic transmission, which is notorious for premature failure. The transmission develops harsh shifting, slipping, and complete failure typically between 60,000-100,000 miles. Internal servo bore wear, solenoid failures, and torque converter issues are common. This is the same problematic transmission used in the Ford Escape and Mercury Cougar of the same era.
before.solution: Change transmission fluid every 30,000 miles with Mercon V. Do NOT flush — drain and fill only to avoid dislodging debris into the valve body. If shifting problems have begun, a solenoid pack replacement ($200-$400) may help temporarily. A rebuilt transmission costs $1,500-$2,500 installed. A used manual transmission swap is popular among enthusiasts as a permanent solution.
symptoms: Check engine light with trans codes

communityRecommendations.content: The CD4E is the Achilles heel of the 1998-2002 626. Change the fluid religiously every 30k miles. Once it starts slipping, you're on borrowed time. Many owners swap to manual to avoid replacing the auto again.
